generic: Ringer's Lactate (Lactated Ringer's / Compound Sodium Lactate / Hartmann's solution)
cls: Balanced crystalloid intravenous fluid - isotonic electrolyte / volume replacement solution
pharm: Provides water and balanced electrolytes (sodium, potassium, calcium, chloride) with lactate as a bicarbonate precursor that is metabolized in the liver to bicarbonate, expanding the extracellular/intravascular volume with an electrolyte composition close to plasma and a lower chloride load than normal saline.
quick: Titrated to clinical need; typical resuscitation bolus 500-1000 mL, then per fluid status
Considered safe; used routinely peripartum and in pregnancy
Caution - contains potassium; risk of hyperkalemia in renal failure/oliguria
Caution in severe hepatic failure - impaired lactate metabolism may worsen acidosis
Volume status, electrolytes (Na/K/Ca/Cl), acid-base, renal function
summary: Ringer's lactate (lactated Ringer's, Hartmann's solution) is an isotonic, balanced crystalloid for intravenous fluid and electrolyte replacement and volume resuscitation. Its electrolyte content approximates plasma (sodium ~130 mmol/L, potassium ~4 mmol/L, calcium ~1.5 mmol/L, chloride ~109 mmol/L) and it contains lactate (~28 mmol/L) which is converted to bicarbonate by the liver, giving it a buffering effect and a lower chloride load than 0.9% sodium chloride. It is widely used for surgical and trauma fluid resuscitation, dehydration, and maintenance, and is generally preferred over large-volume normal saline because it avoids hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. Cautions include the potassium and calcium content (calcium is incompatible with ceftriaxone and with blood given through the same line, and can precipitate with certain drugs), and impaired lactate metabolism in severe liver failure. It is dosed by titration to the patient's clinical and laboratory status.
indications: Replacement of extracellular fluid and electrolyte losses (dehydration, vomiting, diarrhea, burns)
Volume resuscitation in hypovolemia, hemorrhage, and shock (as a balanced crystalloid)
Intraoperative and perioperative fluid maintenance and replacement
Source of bicarbonate (via lactate) in mild metabolic acidosis

dosage.d: 500-1000 mL bolus, repeated and titrated to hemodynamic response and fluid status
dosage.n: Reassess after each bolus; avoid fluid overload

dosage.d: Rate and volume individualized to fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base requirements
dosage.n: Adjust to losses and clinical status

dosage.d: Typically 10-20 mL/kg bolus, repeated as needed per resuscitation protocol
Individualized by weight and clinical needs
dosage.n: Monitor closely - children are prone to fluid/electrolyte imbalance and hyponatremia

admin: Administer intravenously through a sterile administration set after visual inspection (use only if clear and the container undamaged)
Do NOT administer simultaneously with, before, or after blood through the same line - the calcium content can cause clotting/precipitation
Do NOT co-administer with ceftriaxone (especially in neonates) - calcium-ceftriaxone precipitation
Use a dedicated line or flush thoroughly when giving incompatible drugs; check drug compatibility before adding to the bag
Control infusion rate; use an infusion pump for precise or pediatric administration and monitor for signs of overload
moa: Ringer's lactate is a balanced crystalloid whose osmolality and electrolyte composition approximate those of plasma, so infused fluid distributes through the extracellular compartment to expand interstitial and intravascular volume. Sodium chloride maintains tonicity and extracellular volume, while potassium and calcium replace physiologic electrolytes. The lactate anion is metabolized, predominantly in the liver, through the gluconeogenic and oxidative pathways to bicarbonate, providing an alkalinizing buffer that helps correct mild metabolic acidosis and avoids the hyperchloremic acidosis associated with large volumes of 0.9% saline.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to sodium lactate or components
Lactated Ringer's should not be administered simultaneously with citrated/anticoagulated blood through the same line (calcium causes coagulation)
Concomitant ceftriaxone in neonates (<=28 days) - risk of fatal calcium-ceftriaxone precipitation
relative: Significant renal impairment / oliguria (potassium load, fluid retention)
Metabolic or respiratory alkalosis (lactate adds base)
Conditions with sodium/fluid retention (heart failure, edema, cirrhosis)
monitor: Fluid balance and signs of overload (pulmonary edema)
Serum electrolytes, especially potassium and sodium
Serum calcium when giving drugs that interact with calcium

preg: Ringer's lactate is considered safe in pregnancy and is used routinely for fluid management during labor and delivery and in obstetric care. Monitor volume status to avoid overload.
lact: Ringer's lactate is compatible with breastfeeding; the electrolytes are physiologic constituents and there is no concern for the nursing infant.
renal: Use with caution in renal impairment or oliguria because of the potassium content (risk of hyperkalemia) and reduced ability to excrete a fluid and sodium load. Monitor potassium, fluid balance, and renal function closely.
hepatic: In severe hepatic impairment the conversion of lactate to bicarbonate is impaired, which can blunt the buffering effect and, with lactic acidosis, may worsen acid-base derangement. Use with caution and monitor acid-base status.

major: Ceftriaxone - forms an insoluble calcium-ceftriaxone precipitate; do not mix or co-administer, especially in neonates
Blood products - the calcium in lactated Ringer's can cause clotting/precipitation if administered through the same line as citrated blood
moderate: Potassium-sparing diuretics, ACE inhibitors/ARBs - additive hyperkalemia risk given the potassium content
Drugs that are physically/chemically incompatible with calcium (e.g., certain phosphate-containing solutions) - precipitation
minor: Lithium - sodium-containing fluids increase renal lithium clearance and may lower lithium levels
interactions.diagnostics: Lactate content can confound serum lactate measurement if sampled near the infusion site; may transiently alter measured electrolytes.

serious: Fluid overload / pulmonary edema with excessive or rapid infusion

monitoring: Fluid balance (intake/output, weight, signs of overload)
Serum electrolytes - sodium, potassium, calcium, chloride
Acid-base status (especially in liver disease or shock)
Infusion site for phlebitis or extravasation
counsel: This is an intravenous fluid given by a nurse or doctor to replace fluids and salts your body needs
Tell the staff if you feel short of breath, notice swelling, or have chest discomfort during the drip
Report pain, swelling, or redness at the drip site
If you have kidney, heart, or liver problems, the team will watch your fluid and salt levels closely
Let staff know all medicines you receive - some cannot be given through the same line
pk: Immediate intravascular volume expansion on infusion
Effect during and immediately after infusion
Crystalloid redistributes from plasma to interstitium within ~20-30 minutes
Short intravascular dwell time; most leaves circulation within an hour
Store at controlled room temperature; do not use if cloudy or seal broken; single-use
pearls: Balanced crystalloid - lactate is metabolized to bicarbonate, avoiding the hyperchloremic acidosis seen with large-volume normal saline
Contains calcium - NEVER infuse through the same line as blood/citrated products or with ceftriaxone (fatal precipitation reported in neonates)
Contains potassium ~4 mmol/L - caution in renal failure and hyperkalemia
Slightly hypotonic relative to plasma; avoid in patients at risk of cerebral edema where isotonic saline may be preferred
Generic balanced crystalloid - no single branded FDA NDA; composition standardized in USP/BNF and EMA-equivalent monographs
Lactate is exogenous, not a marker of tissue hypoperfusion - interpret serum lactate cautiously during infusion
missed: Not applicable - Ringer's lactate is an intravenous fluid administered and titrated by clinical staff according to the patient's fluid and electrolyte needs.
overdose: Excessive administration causes fluid overload (pulmonary edema, heart failure), dilution and electrolyte disturbances (hypernatremia, hyperkalemia, hypercalcemia), and metabolic alkalosis from excess lactate. Stop or slow the infusion, reassess fluid and electrolyte status, and treat with diuretics, electrolyte correction, and supportive measures; dialysis may be needed in renal failure.
